stem:
Masvingo Steel Fabricators has two production departments, Machining and Welding, and a Stores department. Annual overheads for 2026:

| Overhead | US\$ | Basis of apportionment or allocation |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Factory rent | 33,000 | Floor area: Machining 440 m², Welding 360 m², Stores 200 m² |
| Depreciation of machinery | 21,000 | Carrying amount: Machining 60%, Welding 30%, Stores 10% |
| Supervisors' salaries | 9,100 | Allocated: Machining US\$5,940, Welding US\$3,160 |
| Storekeepers' wages | 6,200 | Allocated to Stores |

The Stores department is used by Machining and Welding in the ratio 60 : 40. Overheads are absorbed in Machining on machine hours (budget 6,000 hours) and in Welding on direct labour hours (budget 7,800 hours).

Actual results for 2026: Machining 6,300 machine hours and overhead US\$43,600; Welding 7,400 direct labour hours and overhead US\$26,780 (both after reapportionment of Stores).

Job FAB22 used direct materials of US\$1,150, 34 direct labour hours at US\$6 an hour (all in Welding) and 24 machine hours in Machining.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the rent apportioned to Welding.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the total overhead of the Stores department before reapportionment.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the Stores overhead reapportioned to Machining.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the total overhead of Machining after reapportionment.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the budgeted absorption rate for:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Machining, per machine hour

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: Welding, per direct labour hour

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Calculate the overhead absorbed by Machining in 2026.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Calculate the under-absorbed overhead in Welding (give the amount only).

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: Calculate the total production cost of Job FAB22.
parts.explanation: Prime cost 1,354; Machining 24 × 7 = 168; Welding 34 × 3.5 = 119; total US\$1,641.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Prime cost 1,354; Machining 24 × 7 = 168; Welding 34 × 3.5 = 119; total US\$1,641.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: The firm wants a profit margin of 20% on the selling price. Calculate the price to quote for Job FAB22.

parts.label: (j)
parts.stem: A customer offers US\$1,900 for Job FAB22. Welding is short of work and overhead is largely fixed. Evaluate whether the firm should accept, referring to your calculations and to non-financial factors.

points.description: The offer of 1,900 is above the full production cost of 1,641 and earns 259
But it is below the target price and gives a margin below 20%
Most overhead is fixed, so the relevant gain is higher than the profit shown by full costing if there is spare capacity
Non-financial: spare capacity in Welding and the chance of repeat orders from the customer
Recommendation: accept if there is spare capacity and no regular work is displaced; otherwise negotiate a higher price

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The offer covers the full production cost of 1,641 and earns 259, though below the 20% margin target. With Welding short of work most of the overhead is incurred anyway, so accepting adds to profit. The firm should accept if no regular work is lost and the customer may order again.

parts.explanation: One mark for each point, up to 5.
hints: Compare the offer with the full cost and the target price.

explanation: This ZIMSEC Paper 3 style cost question tests the overhead analysis, absorption rates, under-absorption, a job cost and a recommendation.
hints: Apportion shared costs on the stated bases.
Reapportion Stores before calculating the rates.

stem:
Zvishavane Paints Ltd makes two products, gloss paint (G) and matt paint (M). Information for 2026:

|  | Gloss (G) | Matt (M) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Units sold | 5,500 | 3,000 |
| Selling price per unit US\$ | 15 | 10 |
| Variable cost per unit (including selling) US\$ | 9 | 6 |

Fixed costs common to both products were US\$28,000. In addition, fixed costs of US\$6,500 are incurred only because matt paint is made, and would be avoided if matt paint stopped being made. The directors have been given a profit statement in which the common fixed costs are shared equally between the products, and they are considering stopping the production of matt paint. Give percentages to one decimal place.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the contribution per unit of gloss paint.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the contribution per unit of matt paint.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the total contribution of the two products.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the profit for the year.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the loss shown for matt paint in the directors' statement (give the amount only), after charging half of the common fixed costs and its own fixed costs.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Calculate the amount by which profit would fall if matt paint were stopped (assume the common fixed costs are unchanged).
parts.explanation: Contribution lost 12,000 less avoidable fixed costs saved 6,500 = US\$5,500.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Contribution lost 12,000 less avoidable fixed costs saved 6,500 = US\$5,500.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Calculate the break-even sales revenue for the business as a whole, assuming that the sales mix stays the same.
parts.explanation: Contribution to sales ratio = 45,000 ÷ 112,500 = 40%. Break-even revenue = 34,500 ÷ 0.40 = US\$86,250.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Contribution to sales ratio = 45,000 ÷ 112,500 = 40%. Break-even revenue = 34,500 ÷ 0.40 = US\$86,250.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: Calculate the margin of safety as a percentage of actual sales revenue.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Advise the directors whether to stop making matt paint. Refer to your figures and to non-financial factors.

points.description: The statement shows a loss of 8,500 only because common fixed costs are shared; these costs do not stop if matt paint stops
Matt paint earns a contribution of 12,000 against avoidable fixed costs of 6,500, so it adds 5,500 to profit
Stopping it would reduce profit from 10,500 to 5,000
Recommend continuing to make matt paint
Non-financial: customers who buy both paints may go elsewhere; the jobs of the matt paint workers; or the capacity could be used for a more profitable product

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Matt paint should be kept. The loss in the statement arises from sharing common fixed costs which continue anyway. It earns a contribution of 12,000, more than the 6,500 of fixed costs avoided, so stopping it would cut profit by 5,500 to 5,000. Customers who buy both paints might also be lost; the position could change if the capacity could be used more profitably.

hints: Which costs would stop if matt paint stopped?

explanation: This ZIMSEC Paper 3 style cost question tests marginal costing, a closure decision, break-even for a mix and advice.
hints: Only avoidable fixed costs are relevant to the closure decision.
The C/S ratio is total contribution ÷ total sales.

stem:
Sibanye Garments in Bulawayo faces three decisions.

**Decision 1: a special order.** The normal price of a school shirt is US\$34, the variable cost US\$19 and the full production cost US\$25. A hospital offers US\$23 a shirt for 640 shirts, which would need extra delivery costing US\$380. The factory has spare capacity.

**Decision 2: make or buy.** The factory makes 9,000 buttons a year at a variable cost of US\$0.60 each. Making them needs a machine operator costing US\$1,950 a year that would be avoided if the buttons were bought. A supplier offers them at US\$0.95 each.

**Decision 3: scarce machine time.** Only 840 sewing machine hours are available each month. Three garments are made:

| Garment | Contribution per unit US\$ | Machine hours per unit | Maximum monthly demand (units) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| S | 7 | 0.50 | 900 |
| D | 24 | 2 | 400 |
| T | 9 | 1 | 360 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the gain in profit from accepting the hospital's order.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the loss that would appear on the order if the full production cost were used (give the amount only).
parts.explanation: (23 - 25) × 640 = (1,280), a loss of US\$1,280; this ignores the fact that fixed overhead is incurred anyway.
parts.workedSolution: 1. (23 - 25) × 640 = (1,280), a loss of US\$1,280; this ignores the fact that fixed overhead is incurred anyway.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the relevant cost of making the buttons.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the saving from making the buttons rather than buying them.
parts.explanation: Buying costs 8,550; making costs 7,350; saving US\$1,200.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Buying costs 8,550; making costs 7,350; saving US\$1,200.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Which garment should be made first when machine time is the limiting factor?

options.rationale: Correct: US\$14 of contribution per machine hour.

options.content: Dresses, because they have the highest contribution per unit
options.rationale: The unit contribution is not the correct ranking when time is scarce.

parts.explanation: Contribution per machine hour: S 7 ÷ 0.5 = 14; D 24 ÷ 2 = 12; T 9 ÷ 1 = 9.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of dresses that can be made after meeting the full demand for shirts.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Calculate the maximum monthly contribution.
parts.explanation: Shirts 900 × 7 = 6,300; dresses 195 × 24 = 4,680; trousers nil; total US\$10,980.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Shirts 900 × 7 = 6,300; dresses 195 × 24 = 4,680; trousers nil; total US\$10,980.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: Advise the directors on each of the three decisions, referring to your calculations and to non-financial factors.

points.description: Order: accept, because it adds 2,180 on relevant costs; the full-cost loss ignores fixed overhead
Order: risk that regular customers learn of the low price; spare capacity must be genuine
Buttons: continue to make them; making saves 1,200 a year
Buttons: buy if the supplier is reliable and the operator can be redeployed to earn more; quality of buttons matters
Machine time: make shirts first, then dresses, for 10,980; no trousers
Machine time: consider extra shifts or hiring time if demand for dresses and trousers can be met profitably
Recommendation is supported by figures and refers to a non-financial factor for each decision

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Accept the order: it adds 2,180, though other customers might demand a low price. Keep making buttons: it saves 1,200 a year unless a reliable supplier lets the operator be redeployed. With scarce machine time make shirts then dresses for 10,980 of contribution; extra hours could be considered if profitable.

parts.explanation: One mark for each point, up to 7.
hints: Use relevant costs for the first two decisions and the ranking per hour for the third.

explanation: This ZIMSEC Paper 3 style cost question tests three short-run decisions and ends with a recommendation.
hints: Fixed overhead absorbed is not relevant to the special order.
Rank by contribution per machine hour.

stem:
Chipinge Joinery makes doors (D) and windows (W). Annual overheads are set-ups US\$28,000 (driver: number of set-ups), quality inspection US\$16,000 (inspections), delivery handling US\$16,000 (deliveries) and general factory costs US\$44,000 (machine hours).

|  | Doors (D) | Windows (W) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Units made and sold | 6,400 | 1,250 |
| Machine hours | 3,000 | 1,000 |
| Set-ups | 8 | 20 |
| Inspections | 30 | 50 |
| Deliveries | 60 | 20 |
| Direct cost per unit US\$ | 28 | 30 |
| Selling price per unit US\$ | 48 | 72 |

The present system absorbs all overhead on machine hours. Give answers to the nearest cent where necessary.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the overhead absorption rate per machine hour under the present system.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the overhead per window under the present system.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the cost driver rate for:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: set-ups

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: inspections

parts.label: (iii)
parts.stem: deliveries

parts.label: (iv)
parts.stem: general factory costs, per machine hour

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the total overhead allocated to windows under activity based costing.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the overhead per window under activity based costing.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Calculate the profit per window under activity based costing.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Why does the present system show windows as more profitable than activity based costing does?

options.content: Windows use more machine hours than doors do
options.rationale: Doors use three times as many machine hours as windows.

options.content: Windows cause most set-ups but use few machine hours
options.rationale: Correct: a machine hour rate under-charges windows for the activities they cause.

options.content: Activity based costing increases the total overhead of the firm
options.rationale: The total overhead is the same under both methods.

options.content: Windows are sold at a lower price than doors are sold
options.rationale: The selling price does not affect the sharing of overhead.

parts.explanation: Windows account for 20 of 28 set-ups and 50 of 80 inspections, but only a quarter of the machine hours.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: The managers believe that windows are very profitable and plan a promotion to sell more. Evaluate this plan using the activity based costing information, and advise on the price of windows. Refer to the effect on profit and to non-financial factors.

points.description: Under the present system the profit per window is 21.20; under ABC it is only 6.00
ABC charges windows 36.00 of overhead against 20.80, because they cause most set-ups and inspections
A promotion to sell more windows would add more set-ups and inspections, so the overhead would rise with sales
Doors are probably over-costed under the present system, so their profit is understated
To earn a 20% margin on the price the windows would need to sell for about 82.50
Recommendation: review the price of windows, reduce set-ups by making larger batches, then decide about the promotion
Non-financial: customers may leave if the price rises, or window customers may also buy doors
Limitation: ABC requires data and judgement about drivers; figures are historical

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The present system overstates the profit on windows (21.20 against 6.00 under ABC) because windows cause most set-ups and inspections but few machine hours. A promotion would add activity costs and little profit. The company should reprice windows (about 82.50 for a 20% margin), try to cut set-ups with larger batches, and consider customer reaction before promoting. ABC data need care, since the drivers rely on judgement.

parts.explanation: One mark for each point, up to 8.
hints: Compare the profit per window under the two methods and think about what drives the cost.

explanation: This Cambridge Paper 4 style question compares traditional absorption costing with activity based costing and ends with an evaluation and advice.
hints: Rate = cost of pool ÷ total driver quantity.
Windows use most of the activities.
